Goodness-of-Fit Test for the Skellam Distribution

Source: R/skellam.test.R
skellam.test.Rd

Tests whether a sample of differences of counts comes from a Skellam distribution, with rates either given or estimated by maximum likelihood.

Usage

skellam.test(
  x,
  lambda1 = NULL,
  lambda2 = NULL,
  statistic = c("pearson", "lr"),
  method = c("bootstrap", "asymptotic"),
  B = 999,
  min.expected = 5
)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector of integers.

lambda1, lambda2

Rates of the hypothesised distribution. If both are NULL (default) they are estimated from x with skellam.fit.

statistic

"pearson" (default) for the Pearson chi-squared statistic or "lr" for the likelihood-ratio (G) statistic.

method

"bootstrap" (default) for a parametric-bootstrap p-value, or "asymptotic" for the chi-squared approximation.

B

Number of bootstrap samples.

min.expected

Minimum expected count per cell; sparse tail cells are merged until every cell reaches it.

Value

An object of class "htest" with the usual components (statistic, parameter: degrees of freedom or B, p.value, method, data.name, and estimate: the rates used), plus observed, expected and cells (a data frame with the limits of each cell).

Details

The integers are grouped into cells so that every cell has an expected count of at least min.expected under the hypothesised (or fitted) distribution: the cells start one per integer, the two end cells take the tails, and the cell with the smallest expected count is merged with its smaller neighbour until all reach the minimum. With \(k\) cells, the statistic is \(X^2 = \sum (O - E)^2 / E\) or \(G = 2 \sum O \log(O/E)\).

p-values. When the rates are given, both statistics are approximately \(\chi^2_{k-1}\). When the rates are estimated from the ungrouped data, the limiting distribution lies between \(\chi^2_{k-3}\) and \(\chi^2_{k-1}\) (Chernoff and Lehmann, 1954), so no chi-squared reference is exact: method = "asymptotic" uses \(k - 3\) degrees of freedom, which tends to reject slightly too often. The default parametric bootstrap avoids the problem: it simulates B samples from the fitted distribution, re-estimates the rates and rebuilds the cells for each, and reports \((1 + \#\{T^* \ge T\})/(B + 1)\). Set a seed for reproducible bootstrap p-values.

References

Chernoff, H. and Lehmann, E. L. (1954) The use of maximum likelihood estimates in \(\chi^2\) tests for goodness of fit. Annals of Mathematical Statistics 25(3), 579-586.

See also

skellam.fit, chisq.test

Examples

set.seed(1)
x <- rpois(500, 4) - rpois(500, 2)
skellam.test(x, B = 199)
#> 
#> 	Skellam goodness-of-fit test (Pearson, parametric bootstrap)
#> 
#> data:  x
#> X-squared = 2.3808, B = 199, p-value = 1
#> sample estimates:
#>  lambda1  lambda2 
#> 3.847458 1.877458 
#> 

# a sample with extra zeros is rejected
z <- x; z[sample(500, 60)] <- 0
skellam.test(z, B = 199)
#> 
#> 	Skellam goodness-of-fit test (Pearson, parametric bootstrap)
#> 
#> data:  z
#> X-squared = 41.32, B = 199, p-value = 0.005
#> sample estimates:
#>  lambda1  lambda2 
#> 3.556766 1.826766 
#> 

# rates given in advance: asymptotic chi-squared with k - 1 df
skellam.test(x, lambda1 = 4, lambda2 = 2, method = "asymptotic")
#> 
#> 	Skellam goodness-of-fit test (Pearson, asymptotic chi-squared)
#> 
#> data:  x
#> X-squared = 4.1428, df = 12, p-value = 0.9807
#> sample estimates:
#> lambda1 lambda2 
#>       4       2 
#>
